guides.title: How to Buy from 1688 Without Speaking Chinese: A Beginner's Playbook
guides.excerpt: 1688 is where China's sellers buy their inventory — cheapest prices, but entirely in Chinese. This playbook shows non-Chinese speakers how to search, vet suppliers, handle MOQs, check quality, and stay safe, including the agent shortcut most beginners actually use.

sections.heading: What 1688 Actually Is (and Isn't)
sections.body: 1688.com is the domestic wholesale marketplace of Alibaba Group — the place where Chinese retailers and resellers buy their inventory. Think of it this way: Alibaba.com is the international, English-language storefront with export-ready suppliers; AliExpress is the retail counter where anyone can buy single units at a markup; 1688 is the back room where the actual wholesale happens, entirely in Chinese, priced in yuan, built for domestic buyers. That is why prices on 1688 are usually the lowest you will find anywhere — you are buying at the same counter as the Chinese sellers who later mark the goods up for export. The trade-off: no English interface, suppliers who assume you read Chinese and pay through Alipay, domestic-only shipping, and minimum order quantities set for businesses, not individuals. It is not a scam site and it is not a secret — it is simply a market that was never designed for you. The good news: with browser translation and the right workflow, a non-Chinese speaker can research products, vet suppliers, and even place orders — or skip the hard parts entirely by using an agent, which we cover in the final section.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Make Translation Your First Tool
sections.body: Before you touch 1688, set up translation. In Chrome, right-click any page and choose Translate to English — the whole interface becomes readable in one click. For searching, do not type English keywords into the 1688 search bar and hope; open a translation tool, type your product keyword in English (say, dog nail grinder), copy the Chinese result, and paste that into the 1688 search box. Save the translations that work in a simple glossary document — you will reuse them constantly. On your phone, a camera-translation app lets you point at packaging, labels, and supplier chat screenshots. Two practical notes: machine translation mangles product names (expect gems like explosive press type concealer), so read for meaning, not poetry; and when messaging suppliers, keep your sentences short and simple — Can I order 50 pieces first? translates far more reliably than a paragraph of conditions. Translation gets you 90 percent of the way there. The remaining 10 percent — payment, domestic shipping, negotiation nuance — is where agents earn their keep.

sections.heading: Step 2 — Find and Vet Suppliers
sections.body: Never buy from the first supplier you find. Search your translated keyword, open five to ten supplier listings, and compare them like a detective. On each supplier page, look for: how many years they have been on the platform, their transaction volume and buyer ratings (1688 shows these as badges and scores — higher and older is generally safer), and whether their product photos look like real factory shots or stolen stock images. Message three or four of them through the platform chat with translation on, and watch response time and clarity — a supplier who answers quickly and directly in simple terms is worth more than one with a slightly lower price who ghosts you. Red flags: prices dramatically below everyone else, refusal to sell samples, no verifiable business information, or pressure to move the conversation off-platform immediately. Always order samples before any bulk order — a $5 sample that reveals bad quality is the cheapest insurance in this business.

sections.heading: Step 3 — Handle MOQs and Negotiation
sections.body: MOQ means minimum order quantity — the smallest batch a supplier will sell you. On 1688, MOQs are set for domestic resellers, so do not be intimidated by a 500-piece MOQ on the listing; it is very often negotiable, especially if you message the supplier directly. Use short translated sentences: Hello, I am a new buyer. Can I start with 100 pieces? Or: What is your best price for 200 pieces? Suppliers deal with new buyers constantly, and many will flex for a first order. Ask about samples in the same message — most suppliers sell samples at a slightly higher per-unit price, which is normal. Two things to nail down before money moves: the exact unit price at your quantity, and what happens with defective items (get the replacement policy in writing in the chat). If negotiation feels overwhelming, this entire step is the number-one reason beginners use a sourcing agent — agents negotiate MOQs and prices in Chinese daily, and their service cost is often offset by the better price they get you.

sections.heading: Step 4 — Quality Control Without Being There
sections.body: You cannot visit the factory, so build quality control into the process. Step one is always samples: order one to three units and inspect them against the listing — materials, function, finish, packaging, and whether the thing actually does what the photos promise. Test electronics through a full charge cycle; wash fabric items once; stress-test anything with a moving part. For larger orders, you have two options: ask your agent to do a pre-shipment check (most agents will photograph or video your goods before they ship — ask for this explicitly), or hire a third-party inspection service for orders large enough to justify the cost. Accept a basic truth: some defect rate is normal in low-cost manufacturing. What separates professionals from gamblers is having the defective-replacement policy agreed before the order, not argued about after. Document everything in the chat — translated chat logs are your contract. When the sample arrives, compare it against the listing photos side by side — differences in color, material, or finish at the sample stage predict exactly what your customers will complain about later.

sections.heading: Step 5 — Use an Agent, and Keep Payments Safe
sections.body: Here is the shortcut most non-Chinese-speaking dropshippers actually use: a sourcing agent. An agent is a company that buys from 1688 on your behalf — in yuan, through domestic payment, from vetted suppliers — then quality-checks the goods, stores them, and ships individual orders to your customers worldwide, usually with no per-order MOQ. CJ Dropshipping is one such agent operating in this space, alongside several others; compare a few on pricing, shipping lines, and support responsiveness before committing. This site's freight data, for example, comes from real CJ shipping quotes, which is why the numbers here reflect what you would actually pay rather than a supplier's optimistic estimate. On payment safety, the rules are simple: keep transactions inside a platform that offers buyer protection, never wire money to a personal bank account no matter how good the deal sounds, use a credit card where possible so you have chargeback rights, and start small — your first order with any new supplier or agent should be an amount you can afford to lose.

guides.title: Landed Cost Explained: The Math Every Dropshipper Gets Wrong
guides.excerpt: Product cost + freight + duties = landed cost — and beginners almost always price off the wrong number. Two worked examples with real data (a $0.25 lamp and a $2.73 dog bed) show why freight, not the sticker price, decides your margin.

sections.heading: The Formula: Product + Freight + Duties = Landed Cost
sections.body: Landed cost is the total amount it costs to get one unit of product into your customer's hands — and it is the only cost number that matters when you set a retail price. The formula is simple: product cost plus international freight plus import duties and taxes equals landed cost. (Some sellers also fold in payment processing fees and packaging; we handle fees separately in the examples below.) Beginners obsess over the product cost — the $0.25 or $2.73 number on the listing — because it is the biggest, most visible figure. But as you will see in the examples, the product cost is often the smallest part of what you actually pay. Freight from China to your market, which depends on weight, package size, and the shipping line you choose, routinely exceeds the product price. Duties and sales taxes vary by country, product category, and declared value — check your country's customs rules rather than guessing. Until you have computed all three, you do not know your cost. Everything in this guide uses real numbers from this site's product data, checked against live freight quotes.

sections.heading: Why a $0.25 Product Can Still Lose You Money
sections.body: Look at the LED night light in our product data. The product costs $0.25. The cheapest freight to Canada is $4.74. Landed cost: $4.99. Freight is 95 percent of what you pay — you are not selling a twenty-five-cent lamp, you are selling a five-dollar delivered package. Now imagine a beginner who sees $0.25 and lists it at $4.99 retail, thinking they have doubled their money. They have made exactly zero — before payment fees, before ads, before the inevitable returns. This is the single most common math error in dropshipping: pricing off the product cost instead of the landed cost. It happens because the product price is quoted everywhere and the freight is buried three clicks deep. The fix is procedural, not intellectual: never set a price until you have written down all three numbers. Cheap products are not automatically profitable products — a $0.25 item with $4.74 freight needs the same $15 retail price as a $5 item with no freight. The product cost is trivia; the landed cost is the business.

sections.heading: Worked Example 1: The $4.99 LED Night Light
sections.body: Let us walk the LED night light all the way to a price tag, using the real data: product cost $0.25, freight $4.74 via CJPacket JYSP Sensitive (7 to 15 days to Canada), landed cost $4.99. (Figures checked 2026-10-05; freight quotes move, so recheck before you commit.) Suppose you retail it at $14.99 — a typical price for this kind of gadget. Gross margin per unit: $14.99 minus $4.99 = $10.00. Now subtract a typical card processing fee — for example, around 2.9% plus $0.30, which on $14.99 is about $0.73 — leaving roughly $9.27. That $9.27 has to cover your advertising cost per order, returns, and finally your profit. If your ads cost you, say, $5 per order (an illustrative example — your actual ad costs depend on your channels and creative), you keep about $4.27 per sale. That is a workable beginner product: nothing spectacular, but the math survives contact with reality. Note what made it work — not the $0.25 product cost, but the discipline of pricing at 3x landed cost and accounting for the fee before celebrating.

sections.heading: Worked Example 2: The $16.53 Plush Dog Bed
sections.body: Now the same exercise with a bulky item — the round plush dog bed. Real data: product cost $2.73, freight $13.80 via CJPacket Eub (4 to 8 days to Canada), landed cost $16.53. The product is eleven times more expensive than the LED light, but the landed cost is only about three times higher — because freight dominates both. At a $39.99 retail price: $39.99 minus $16.53 = $23.46 gross; minus the card fee of about $1.46 (2.9% plus $0.30 on $39.99) = roughly $22.00 before ads. With the same illustrative $5 ad cost per order, you keep about $17 per sale — four times the LED light's profit, on a product that costs only $2.73. Two lessons here. First, absolute profit per sale matters more than margin percentage: a 2.4x markup on the dog bed beats 3x on the lamp in dollars. Second, bulky freight is not a dealbreaker if the category supports the retail price — pet owners happily pay $39.99 for their dog's comfort, which is why the category absorbs a $13.80 freight bill that would kill a novelty gadget.

sections.heading: How to Use This Site's Calculator
sections.body: This site exists so you never have to do this math blind. Here is how to use the calculator: pick a product and you will see its real unit cost alongside real freight quotes to Canada — multiple carriers, each with its price and delivery window, checked against live data (currently dated 2026-10-05). Compare the lines the way a professional would: the cheapest line is not always the best — a $1 more expensive line that arrives in 6 days instead of 15 can easily pay for itself in conversion rate. Add your own estimate for duties and taxes based on your country's rules, enter the retail price you are considering, and the calculator shows your margin after the card fee. Use it comparatively: run the same retail price against two or three similar products and let the landed-cost ranking tell you which one deserves your ad budget. And treat every quote as a snapshot — freight prices move with fuel costs, seasons, and carrier capacity, so recheck the numbers before you scale any product, not just when you first discover it.

sections.heading: Five Margin Mistakes Beginners Make
sections.body: Five mistakes that quietly eat beginners' margins. One: pricing off the product cost — covered above, but it deserves repetition because everyone does it once. Two: forgetting return freight. A returned item often costs you the outbound freight twice (there and back) plus a refund; on a $13.80-freight dog bed, one return wipes out the profit of nearly one sale. Price with a returns buffer, or tighten your product page until returns are rare. Three: always picking the slowest freight line to save a dollar. If the $4.74 line takes 15 days and a $5.50 line takes 7, the faster line's conversion lift usually dwarfs the $0.76 — test it rather than assuming. Four: ignoring dimensional weight. Carriers charge by whichever is greater: actual weight or size-derived weight. A 468-gram dog bed in a big box can be billed like a much heavier item — always check the package dims, not just the grams. Five: treating quotes as permanent. Freight is a market, not a menu; recheck before every reorder.
